=================== NODEJS.md
# Node.js Backend Rules

Priority: user instruction > repo conventions > this file. `Never` = hard rule.
Versions: use the Node version, package manager, and module system (ESM or CommonJS) the repo declares (`package.json`, `.nvmrc`, lockfile). Never mix module systems or package managers. Never deprecated APIs.
Default stack (only if the repo has none): TypeScript strict, Fastify, Zod, PostgreSQL with a typed query layer, pino, Vitest, ESLint.

## Checks
- Done only when this passes (or the repo's own scripts): `tsc --noEmit && eslint . && vitest run`, plus the production build.
- Never `any`, `@ts-ignore`, `eslint-disable`, or non-null `!` without a written reason. Never leave `console.log`.
- ESLint is type-aware (typescript-eslint strict) with `no-shadow`, `no-floating-promises`, `no-explicit-any`, and `no-unused-vars` as errors.

## TypeScript
- `strict` and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` on. `unknown` and narrowing instead of `any`.
- Validate every external input with a schema at the boundary: HTTP input, environment, queue messages, database JSON, third-party responses. Infer types from schemas.
- Discriminated unions for results and states. `as const` objects instead of `enum`.
- Production runs the built output. Path aliases must resolve at runtime, not only in the type checker.

## Event Loop and Async
- Never block the event loop: no `*Sync` filesystem, crypto, or child-process calls on request paths, no CPU-heavy loops, no huge `JSON.parse` / `JSON.stringify`. Move CPU work to worker threads or a job queue.
- Every promise is awaited or handled. `unhandledRejection` and `uncaughtException` log and exit; the supervisor restarts the process.
- Independent work runs with `Promise.all` under a concurrency limit. Never an unbounded `Promise.all` over a large list. Never sequential `await` in a loop by accident.
- Never pass an async callback to `forEach`. Use `for...of` or `Promise.all(items.map(...))`.
- Inside `try`, `return await` the promise so `catch` sees its rejection.
- Every outbound call has a timeout and cancellation (`AbortSignal.timeout`).
- Streams for large payloads through `pipeline()` from `stream/promises`. Never `.pipe()` without error handling. Never buffer whole files or uploads in memory.
- Every `EventEmitter` has an `error` listener. Async listeners catch their own errors.
- No request data in module-level variables; concurrent requests share them. Request context uses `AsyncLocalStorage`.
- In-memory caches and maps are bounded (max size and TTL). Listeners and timers are removed when done.

## HTTP Service
- Layers: routes (thin) -> services (business rules) -> repositories (data). Request and response objects never enter services.
- `app` is built by a factory without listening; `server` starts it. Dependencies are passed in at that composition root.
- Schemas validate params, query, body, and headers and reject unknown fields. Responses are serialized through schemas.
- One error handler maps typed errors to status codes with one body shape. Never send stack traces.
- Async route errors must reach the error handler: use a framework version that forwards rejections, or wrap handlers.
- Server timeouts are set. Keep-alive timeout is longer than the load balancer's idle timeout.
- Body size limits, pagination with a max size, security headers, CORS allowlist.
- Rate limits use a shared store when more than one instance runs. Configure trusted proxies so client IPs are correct.
- Graceful shutdown on `SIGTERM`: fail readiness, stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close pools and queues, exit, with a forced deadline.
- Processes are stateless: no in-memory sessions. Scale with processes or containers.
- Environment is parsed and validated once at startup into a typed config. Never read `process.env` elsewhere.
- Structured JSON logs to stdout with a request id and redaction of secrets and PII.

## Data
- One bounded connection pool per process. Pool size times instances stays under the database limit.
- Bound parameters only. Never template-string SQL or unsafe raw-query helpers with user input.
- Inside a transaction every query uses the transaction client. Transactions are short and contain no network calls.
- Prevent N+1: joins, includes, or batched loaders. Select only needed columns. Keyset pagination.
- Migrations are versioned files applied as a deploy step. Never schema sync, push, or development migrate commands in production.
- Money is integer minor units or a decimal type, never a float. Identifiers beyond 2^53 travel as strings.
- Timestamps are UTC ISO strings at the boundary.
- Side-effecting `POST`s accept an idempotency key. Uniqueness is enforced by constraints and upsert.
- Jobs run on a durable queue with retries, backoff, and a dead-letter queue. Never `setTimeout` or in-process cron for work that must not be lost; scheduled jobs run on one instance under a lock.

## Security
- Object-level authorization in services. Never spread a request body into a database write; pick allowed fields.
- Prototype pollution: never deep-merge untrusted objects; reject `__proto__` and `constructor` keys; use `Map` for user-keyed data.
- Query-operator injection: check that values are primitives before they reach a document-database query.
- Never `eval`, `new Function`, or `vm` on untrusted input. Child processes use `execFile` or `spawn` with an argument array.
- User-influenced paths are resolved and checked against a base directory. User-supplied URLs are fetched only from an allowlist.
- No user-supplied regular expressions. Cap input length before matching.
- Passwords use argon2 or bcrypt (async). Tokens come from `crypto.randomBytes` and compare with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. Never `Math.random()` for security.
- JWT verification fixes the algorithm and checks audience, issuer, and expiry. Session cookies are `httpOnly`, `secure`, `sameSite`.
- Install from the lockfile (`npm ci`). Verify package names before adding. Audit in CI. Review install scripts.
- Run as a non-root user with `NODE_ENV=production` and production dependencies only.

## Performance
- Measure with CPU profiles, flame graphs, and event-loop delay. Alert on event-loop lag.
- Reuse connections (keep-alive agents). Size the heap limit to the container.

## Testing
- Services are unit-tested with fakes. Routes are tested through HTTP injection against a real database in a container.
- Fake timers instead of sleeps. Outbound HTTP is faked at the network boundary.
- Each test isolates its data. Tests close servers, pools, and timers so the runner exits.
=================== REACT.md
# React Frontend Rules

Priority: user instruction > repo conventions > this file. `Never` = hard rule.
Versions: use what the repo pins. Read `package.json` before using a version-specific API. Prefer current APIs; never deprecated ones.
Default stack (only if the repo has none): TypeScript strict, Vite, TanStack Query, React Router, React Hook Form, Zod, Tailwind, Vitest.

## Checks
- Done only when this passes (or the repo's own scripts): `tsc --noEmit && eslint . && vitest run && vite build`.
- Never `@ts-ignore`, `eslint-disable`, or `any` without a written reason. Never leave `console.log`.
- ESLint is type-aware (typescript-eslint strict) with `no-shadow`, `no-floating-promises`, `no-explicit-any`, `no-unused-vars`, and `react-hooks` rules as errors.

## Idioms
- One component = one purpose. One hook = one concern.
- Composition (children, slots) over boolean-prop configuration.
- Pure render: no side effects, mutation, `Date.now()`, or `Math.random()` in render.
- Decoupling: UI components do not know where data comes from. Features talk through public exports only.
- Dependency injection: collaborators arrive through props, hook parameters, or context. Wrap globals (`window`, `localStorage`, clock) in a hook or module; never touch them directly in components.
- Resource lifetime (RAII): whatever an effect acquires (listener, timer, subscription, request, object URL) the same effect's cleanup releases.
- Reusability: move code to `shared` on the third use. Shared components take data through props, hold no feature knowledge, and fetch nothing.

## Architecture
- Feature-first: `src/app` (entry, providers, router), `src/features/<name>/{components,hooks,api,types}`, `src/shared/{ui,hooks,lib}`.
- Import direction: `app -> features -> shared`. Never import another feature's internals; use its `index.ts`.
- Layers: components (UI) / hooks (logic) / api (IO). Never call `fetch` inside a component.
- One component per file. Split files over ~200 lines.
- Next.js only: Server Components by default; `"use client"` at leaf components; fetch on the server; no browser-only values during render (hydration mismatch).

## TypeScript
- `strict` and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` on.
- Never `as` casts to silence errors or non-null `!`. Use `unknown` and narrow.
- Validate all external data (API, storage, URL, forms) with a schema at the boundary. Infer types from schemas.
- Model variants and async state as discriminated unions. Never combine boolean flags.
- `as const` objects instead of `enum`. No `React.FC`.

## State
- Use the lowest scope that works: local state -> lifted -> URL -> context -> store.
- Server data lives only in the query cache. Never copy it into `useState` or a store.
- Derive values during render. Never store derived state or mirror props in state.
- Filters, pagination, tabs, and selected ids live in the URL.
- Context only for low-frequency values (auth, theme, locale). Split contexts by concern.
- Update state immutably.

## Hooks and Effects
- Effects only synchronize with external systems (subscriptions, DOM, timers).
- Never use effects for derived state, event logic, or data fetching.
- Every effect has complete deps and cleanup. Never disable `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps`.
- Reset component state with `key`, not an effect.
- No `useMemo`/`useCallback`/`memo` by default. Add after profiling or to stabilize deps. Skip if React Compiler is on.

## Data Fetching
- One typed API client: base URL from env, auth, timeout, normalized errors.
- The API client refreshes an expired session once and queues concurrent requests behind it.
- Query-key factory per feature. Pass the abort `signal` to every request.
- Mutations invalidate or update exact keys. Optimistic updates include rollback.
- Handle all four states: loading, error, empty, success.
- Paginate lists. Debounce search. Never fetch in a loop.
- Live connections (WebSocket, SSE) reconnect with backoff and refetch on reconnect.

## Components
- Stable `key` from data ids. Never array index for dynamic lists.
- Never define a component inside another component.
- Never render `count && <X />`; use a ternary or boolean.
- Forms: schema-validated, field errors shown, submit disabled while pending.
- Dates, numbers, and currency are formatted through `Intl`, never by hand.
- Styling: one system only, design tokens, mobile-first. Inline `style` only for dynamic values.

## Accessibility
- Semantic HTML first (`button`, `a`, `label`, `nav`, `main`). ARIA only when no native element exists.
- Every interactive element: keyboard reachable, visible focus, accessible name.
- Inputs have labels. Errors linked with `aria-describedby`. Images have `alt`.
- Manage focus on dialogs and route changes. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- Never put `onClick` on a `div` or `span`.

## Performance
- Route-level `lazy` + `Suspense`.
- Virtualize lists over ~100 rows.
- Images: explicit dimensions, lazy loading, modern formats.
- Keep state close to where it is used. Pass primitives or stable references.
- Import only what is used. Check bundle cost before adding a library.
- Mark expensive non-urgent updates as transitions or deferred values.

## Errors
- Error boundary per route and per risky widget, with fallback and retry.
- Boundaries do not catch event-handler or async errors. Handle those where they occur.
- One error shape from the API client. User-safe message in UI; details in logs.
- Never write an empty `catch`.

## Security
- Never `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with unsanitized input.
- Never render user, API, or LLM content as HTML or Markdown without sanitizing.
- Never put secrets in client code or public env vars. Everything shipped is public.
- Auth tokens in httpOnly cookies. Never in `localStorage`.
- Reject `javascript:` URLs from user input. External `target="_blank"` gets `rel="noopener noreferrer"`.
- No inline scripts, `eval`, or `new Function`. Stay compatible with a strict CSP.
- Client-side permission checks are UX only. The backend enforces authorization.
- Install from the committed lockfile (`npm ci`). Dependency audit shows no high or critical findings.
- Patch one package at a time, run the checks, commit alone.

## Testing
- Vitest + React Testing Library + `user-event`. Network faked with MSW.
- Query by role, label, or text. `data-testid` is the last resort.
- Never test internal state, class names, or component internals.
- Async UI: `findBy*` or `waitFor`. Never fixed timeouts.
- Shared `renderWithProviders` helper: real providers, fresh query client per test, retries off.
- Cover loading, error, empty, and success states; user interactions; form validation.
- `renderHook` only for hooks with non-trivial logic.
- Test files colocated: `Component.test.tsx`. E2E (Playwright) for critical flows only.
=================== UIUX.md
# UI/UX Rules

Priority: user instruction > repo conventions > this file. `Never` = hard rule.
Platform-agnostic: web, desktop, mobile. Use the product's design system and components first. On native platforms follow the platform guidelines before inventing a pattern.

## Checks
- Done only when every screen has been looked at rendered (screenshot or device), not only read as code.
- Each screen works by keyboard alone, with a screen reader, at 200% text size, at the smallest supported width, and in light and dark themes.
- An automated accessibility check is clean. Contrast meets WCAG AA.
- Every data view implements loading, empty, error, and success states.

## UX
How users think, decide and succeed: research, flows, heuristics.

### Method
- Start from the user's task: who, what goal, what counts as success. Design the task flow before the screen.
- Evidence ranks: user research and usage data, then established heuristics, then platform conventions, then opinion. Never claim what users want without evidence; mark assumptions that need user validation.
- Before done, run a heuristic evaluation (Nielsen's ten, below) and a cognitive walkthrough of the primary task: at each step, does the user know what to do, see how, and understand the result?
- Humans validate with usability tests of about five users per round, then iterate.
- Measure key tasks: completion rate, time on task, error rate. Product level: HEART. Perceived usability: SUS. Instrument the events.
- Uncertain changes ship as an A/B test behind a flag, with the metric chosen in advance.

### Usability Heuristics (Nielsen)
- Visibility of system status: feedback within 100 ms; over 1 s show progress; over 10 s show progress with cancel.
- Match the real world: the user's words and concepts. Never internal jargon.
- User control and freedom: undo, cancel, back, and a clear exit from every flow.
- Consistency and standards: the same thing looks and behaves the same everywhere. Reuse components; never restyle one-off.
- Error prevention: constraints and good defaults beat error messages. Destructive actions are undoable or confirmed.
- Recognition over recall: show options, history, and context. Never make the user remember across screens.
- Flexibility and efficiency: shortcuts, bulk actions, and saved defaults for experts, invisible to novices.
- Aesthetic and minimalist design: one primary action per screen; remove what does not serve the task.
- Help users recover from errors: say what happened and how to fix it, keep their input, offer retry. Never raw error codes or blame.
- Help and documentation: in context, searchable, task-focused.

### Laws and Effects
- Jakob's law: users expect your product to work like the ones they already know. Use familiar patterns.
- Fitts's law: primary and frequent targets are large and close to the pointer or thumb; destructive ones sit apart.
- Hick's law: fewer choices per step, a recommended default, progressive disclosure for advanced options.
- Miller's law: short-term memory holds only a few items. Chunk content into small groups; never make the user hold information in mind.
- Tesler's law: complexity that cannot be removed is absorbed by the system, not pushed to the user.
- Postel's law: accept loosely formatted input; be strict in what you show and store.
- Doherty threshold: keep interaction responses under 400 ms.
- Gestalt: proximity, similarity, common region, and alignment express grouping. Whitespace separates groups.
- Von Restorff effect: only the primary action is visually distinct.
- Serial position effect: the most important items go first or last in a list or menu.
- Peak-end rule: polish the hardest moment and the final step of a flow.
- Goal-gradient effect: show progress in multi-step tasks.
- Aesthetic-usability effect: polish raises tolerance for flaws; it never replaces usability testing.
- Norman's principles: signifiers show what is interactive, mappings are natural, constraints block wrong actions.

## UI
How the interface looks, behaves and is built.

### Layout
- Hierarchy comes from size, weight, and spacing before color.
- Spacing, sizes, and radii come from the token scale. Never arbitrary pixel values.
- Responsive from the smallest width up. No horizontal scrolling at 320 CSS px.
- Body line length 45 to 75 characters.
- Touch targets at least 44 by 44 pt (48 dp), with space between them.
- Reserve space for images and async content so the layout never shifts. Skeletons match the final layout.
- Respect safe areas. The on-screen keyboard never covers the focused field.
- Design with real and extreme content: long names, empty lists, huge numbers, translated text 40% longer, right-to-left.

### Typography and Color
- Type sizes from the scale, at most two families, body at least 16 px on the web. Relative units so user font settings apply.
- Tabular figures and right alignment for numeric columns.
- Components use semantic color tokens (`text-primary`, `surface`, `danger`), never raw hex. Dark mode comes from tokens, not inversion.
- Contrast: 4.5:1 for text; 3:1 for large text, UI components, and focus indicators.
- Never color alone to carry meaning. Pair it with text, an icon, or a pattern.
- Hover, focus, active, selected, disabled, and error states are visibly distinct.

### Components and Interaction
- Buttons act; links navigate. Button labels are verbs naming the outcome ("Save changes", never "OK").
- Destructive actions are visually separate from the primary action and name the object ("Delete project Alpha").
- Loading: skeletons for content, spinners for short waits, progress bars for long ones. Never freeze the interface. Block double submission.
- Empty states say what belongs here and offer the first action.
- Modals are rare: focus is trapped, `Esc` closes, focus returns to the trigger. Never stacked, never on page load.
- Toasts are for non-critical confirmations, never the only place an error or required action appears.
- Navigation shows where the user is. Back works. URLs or deep links restore the view, including filters and scroll position.
- Tables and lists provide sort, filter, and pagination or virtualization, with a small-screen strategy.
- Search is debounced, shows the query and result count, and guides on no results.
- Disabled controls explain why, or stay enabled and validate on use.

### Forms
- Every field has a visible label above it. A placeholder is never the label.
- Ask only for what is needed. Mark optional fields. One column.
- Correct input type, keyboard, and `autocomplete`.
- Validate on blur and on submit, not on each keystroke. Messages sit next to the field and say how to fix it.
- On submit failure focus the first error and keep every value.
- Never block paste. Offer show-password. State password rules up front.
- Long forms autosave or warn before unsaved changes are lost.
- Multi-step flows allow going back without loss and end with a review.

### Accessibility
- WCAG level AA is the bar: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust.
- Native elements first. ARIA only to fill gaps, with correct role, name, and state.
- Everything is operable by keyboard in a logical order with a visible focus indicator. No keyboard traps. Never remove the focus outline without a replacement.
- Icon-only controls have accessible names. Meaningful images have alt text; decorative ones have empty alt.
- Headings are hierarchical. Landmarks mark regions. Async updates are announced through live regions.
- Form errors are programmatically tied to their fields.
- After navigation or a dynamic view change, move focus to the new content.
- Respect reduced-motion and high-contrast settings. Nothing flashes more than three times a second.
- Content reflows at 200% zoom. Orientation is not locked. Hover-only content is also reachable by focus and touch.
- Media has captions. Time limits can be extended.
- Test with a keyboard and a screen reader; automated tools find only part of the problems.

### Motion
- Motion explains cause and effect. UI transitions take 150 to 300 ms and never block input.
- Animate transform and opacity only.

### Content
- Users scan, they do not read: front-load headings and first words, one idea per paragraph, lists for steps.
- Plain language, sentence case, one term per concept, specific over vague.
- No hard-coded user-facing strings. Never build sentences by concatenation; use messages with plurals and placeholders.
- Dates, numbers, and currency are localized and unambiguous. Layout uses logical (start/end) properties.

### Performance and Resilience
- Web pages stay in the good range of Core Web Vitals: LCP under 2.5 s, INP under 200 ms, CLS under 0.1.
- Show useful content progressively. Lazy-load what is off screen. Size images for the device.
- Slow and offline networks are designed for: timeouts, retry, and cached content marked as stale.

### Design System
- Tokens for color, spacing, type, radius, shadow, motion, and z-index. Components consume tokens only.
- New needs become component variants, not local overrides.
- One icon set at consistent size and stroke, with text labels unless the icon is universal.

### Trust
- Never dark patterns: pre-checked consent, hidden costs, confirm-shaming, hard-to-cancel flows.
- Ask for a permission in context, with the reason, at the moment it is needed.
- Consent is opt-in and as easy to withdraw as to give.

# AGENTS.md

Working rules for AI agents and people in this repo. **Draft: this will evolve as the product grows.** If a rule is wrong or in the way, say so and propose a change instead of working around it.

Priority: user instruction > this file and `docs/` > `guidelines/`. `Never` = hard rule. The full general guidelines are in `guidelines/` (CODING, NODEJS, REACT, UIUX); this file is the project-adapted distillation. **Do not read `guidelines/` by default**; open one only when this file is silent on something.

## Project in one paragraph

A browser-based Markdown editor where an AI co-author flags and suggests; the user always sees a diff and must Accept. React + Vite + TipTap front end, a small Hono proxy to OpenRouter, localStorage persistence, no auth, no database. Pre-implementation: decisions exist, code does not yet.

## Source of truth

Read only what the task needs, not everything.

| Need | File |
|---|---|
| What the product does (D1-D17 editor, H1-H7 home) | `docs/PRODUCT-DIRECTION.md` |
| Stack, AI contract, storage, security, structure, packages, gates (T1-T13) | `docs/TECHNICAL-DIRECTION.md` |
| Tokens, components, licenses, responsive (S1-S9) | `docs/DESIGN-DIRECTION.md` |

Product decisions are settled. Do not re-open them; if code contradicts one, flag it. Cite decision IDs (`D4`, `H5`, `T7`, `S8`) in code comments and test names.

## Project rules

1. **Nothing changes the document without Accept** (T3). Suggestions are decorations; Accept is one transaction.
2. **Contracts live in `shared/schemas/`** as zod, types from `z.infer` (T11). Never hand-duplicate a type.
3. **The OpenRouter key never reaches the browser** (T4). Model names come from config, never from the client (T7).
4. **Model output is untrusted** (T10): validate with zod, render as text only, drop responses whose paragraph hash no longer matches.
5. **Feature code imports UI only from `src/design-system/`**, never `@atlaskit/*` or icon packages directly (S8).
6. **Only permissive licenses** (Apache-2.0, MIT, ISC, BSD). `@atlaskit/icon` and `@atlaskit/logo` are banned; icons are Lucide or custom SVG (S6, S8).
7. **No hover-only affordances**; every interaction has a touch and keyboard path (S9, D17).
8. **No test calls the real model** (T9). Never commit `.env` or secrets. Never log document text or the API key.

## The gate

One command, `pnpm check`, runs: format check, type-aware strict ESLint, `tsc --noEmit`, license check (S8), Vitest, production build (web and server). **It is created before any feature code.**

- Done only when `pnpm check` passes. Fix causes; never suppress errors or warnings (`@ts-ignore`, `eslint-disable`, `any`, non-null `!` need a written reason).
- After every change run the fast checks (format, lint, types). Run tests by scope: affected tests per step, the full suite once before push or done.
- ESLint errors on: undeclared and unused names, shadowing, floating promises, explicit `any`, missing types, `react-hooks` violations, deep imports across features, direct `@atlaskit/*` imports. No `console.log` left behind.
- Report what was run and the real result. Never claim unverified work passes.

## Packages (T12)

- **pnpm only.** Never npm or yarn; never commit another lockfile. Commands: `pnpm dev`, `pnpm test`, `pnpm check`.
- **Exact versions only.** `.npmrc` has `save-exact=true`. No `^`, `~`, ranges or `latest`, dev dependencies included. `packageManager` and `engines` pin pnpm and Node.
- Commit `pnpm-lock.yaml`; install with `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`.
- Adding a dependency: first prefer the platform, the standard library or code we already have. Verify the exact name exists and is maintained, check its license (S8), add one package at a time, run `pnpm check`, commit alone.
- Upgrading: deliberate, one package at a time, license re-checked, checks run, committed alone. `pnpm audit` shows no high or critical findings.
- Dependency install scripts stay blocked unless explicitly allowlisted with a reason.
- Wrap third-party libraries in an adapter when they touch domain logic (AI provider, storage, design system).

## Coding rules

- Read related files before editing; match existing patterns, naming and style. Take the first option that works: not needed -> reuse -> standard library -> platform feature -> installed dependency -> small edit -> new minimal code.
- Smallest diff that fully solves the task. Never refactor, rename or reformat unrelated code. Before changing a signature or schema, find and update every caller.
- Never leave TODOs, stubs, mock data, dead code, commented-out code or debug output. A deliberate shortcut gets one `DEBT:` comment with its limit and when to revisit.
- Never invent APIs, flags or package names; verify in the repo, lockfile or docs. Never deprecated APIs.
- Bug: reproduce it, fix the root cause, not the symptom. Stuck after two attempts at the same fix: stop, report what failed, propose options.
- Ambiguous requirement: pick the simplest option and state the assumption.
- KISS, YAGNI. Abstract on the third repetition; duplication beats a wrong abstraction. One responsibility per function and module. Pure core, side effects at the edges. Composition over inheritance.
- Functions: one level of abstraction, guard clauses over nesting (at most ~3 levels), at most ~4 parameters, no boolean flag parameters, no hidden inputs or outputs.
- Names state intent; units in the name (`timeout_ms`); no magic numbers or strings. No `utils`/`helpers` dumping grounds: name modules by what they own (`diff`, `hash`).
- Types: strictest checking, no escape hatches. Parse external data at the boundary (API, storage, environment) into validated types, then trust them. Discriminated unions instead of flag combinations; `as const` objects instead of `enum`; immutable by default.
- Errors: never swallow (no empty `catch`). Expected failures are typed results; exceptions are for bugs. Messages state what failed, without secrets. Handle edges: empty, missing, zero, duplicate, non-ASCII.
- Never global mutable state or side effects at import time. Inject IO, clock, randomness and environment at the edges; wrap `window`, `localStorage` and the clock in a module or hook.
- Whatever a scope acquires (listener, timer, request, subscription) the same scope releases, on every path.
- Bound everything: input size, retries, timeouts, caches. Measure before optimizing.
- Comments explain why, not what. Document public APIs: purpose, inputs, errors.

## Frontend rules (React)

- Feature-first per T11: components (UI) / hooks (logic) / API client (IO). Never `fetch` in a component. One component per file; split files over ~200 lines. Never define a component inside another.
- Import direction: `app -> features -> design-system / lib`. Other features are reached only through their `index.ts`.
- TypeScript `strict` and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. No `as` casts to silence errors, no `React.FC`. Variants and async state (idle, loading, ready, error) are discriminated unions.
- State at the lowest scope that works: local -> lifted -> URL -> context -> Zustand. Derive values in render; never mirror props or derived data in state. Editor-internal state belongs to the ProseMirror plugins (T3), not React state.
- Effects only synchronize with external systems and always have full deps and cleanup. Never use effects for derived state, event logic or fetching. Reset with `key`. No `useMemo`/`useCallback`/`memo` by default; add after profiling.
- AI calls go through the typed client in `features/ai`: timeout, abort `signal` on every request, one normalized error shape. Handle loading, error, empty and success. AI failure shows the D14 status and never breaks the editor.
- Stable `key` from ids, never the index. Never render `count && <X />`. Dates, numbers and relative times through `Intl`.
- Error boundary per route and around the editor, with fallback and retry. Boundaries do not catch event-handler or async errors; handle those where they occur.
- Security: never `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`; never render user, API or LLM content as HTML or Markdown without sanitizing (T10). No secrets in client code. External `target="_blank"` gets `rel="noopener noreferrer"`. No inline scripts, `eval` or `new Function`.
- Route-level `lazy` + `Suspense`; check bundle cost before adding a library.
- Tests: Vitest + React Testing Library + `user-event`, colocated as `Component.test.tsx`. Query by role, label or text (`data-testid` last). Never test internal state or class names. `findBy*`/`waitFor` and fake timers (for the D4 pause), never fixed sleeps. The AI is faked at the client boundary. Cover loading, error, empty and success.

## Server rules (Hono, Node)

- ESM only. Layers: route (thin) -> AI service -> `AIProvider`. Request and response objects never enter the service. The app is built by a factory with its dependencies passed in (`createApp(deps)`); a separate entrypoint listens.
- Validate body, params and query with zod at the boundary, reject unknown fields, and serialize responses through schemas (T5).
- Environment is parsed once at startup into a typed config; never read `process.env` elsewhere (T7). Fail fast on missing config.
- One error handler maps typed errors to status codes with one body shape; never send stack traces. Out-of-credit maps to the D14 status.
- Every outbound call has a timeout (`AbortSignal.timeout`) and is cancelled when the client disconnects. Retries are bounded (T5: one).
- Never block the event loop: no `*Sync` calls on request paths. Every promise is awaited or handled; `return await` inside `try`.
- Body size limit and model allowlist enforced here (T7). CORS: same-origin through the Vite proxy; allow only the local dev origin.
- Structured logs to stdout with secrets and document text redacted. Never `eval`, `new Function` or `vm`.
- Tests: the service is unit-tested with a fake `AIProvider`; routes through Hono's in-process request against the factory app. Tests close what they open.

## UI/UX rules

- **Done means seen.** Every screen is looked at rendered (screenshot in the browser pane), not only read as code. Check at 360, 768 and 1280px, light and dark, keyboard only, and 200% zoom. Accessibility check clean once automated (axe or similar); until then a manual keyboard and screen-reader pass. Contrast meets WCAG AA.
- Every data view has loading, empty, error and success states (H6, D14).
- Heuristics that matter here: visible system status (feedback in 100 ms, progress after 1 s, e.g. the card spinner); user control (Accept, Dismiss, Esc, single-step undo D17); error prevention (destructive actions confirm and name the object, H5); recovery (say what happened and how to fix, keep the user's input); consistency (reuse design-system components, never restyle one-off); minimal (one primary action per screen).
- Layout: spacing, sizes and radii from tokens only (S2). No horizontal scroll at 320px; fully usable from 360px (S9). Document text at least 16px with 45-75 characters per line; UI chrome follows the ADS scale. Touch targets at least 44x44 on coarse pointers. Reserve space for async content so layout never shifts.
- Color: semantic tokens only, never raw hex; never color alone to carry meaning (S7). Hover, focus, active, selected, disabled and error states are visibly distinct.
- Buttons act, links navigate; button labels are verbs naming the outcome. Modals are rare (delete confirm only): focus trapped, `Esc` closes, focus returns to the trigger. No toast as the only place an error appears.
- **Disabled controls: the product record wins.** H2 and H3 keep visible, disabled items (a promise of future features); give each a small "Soon" label or tooltip so it explains itself.
- Accessibility: semantic HTML first, ARIA only to fill gaps. Everything reachable and operable by keyboard with a visible focus ring; icon-only controls have accessible names; headings and landmarks are hierarchical; async updates use live regions; hover content is also reachable by focus and touch. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- Motion explains cause and effect: 150-300 ms, transform and opacity only, never blocking input.
- Content: plain language, sentence case, one term per concept. The AI speaks in neutral, factual one-liners (D8). Never put a placeholder where a label belongs.

## Dropped on purpose (does not fit this project yet)

Revisit when the product grows (Phase 2: sign-in, sync, real users).

- **Server:** PostgreSQL and the data layer, migrations, idempotency keys, durable job queues, authentication and authorization (JWT, passwords, sessions, cookies), multi-instance concerns (shared rate-limit store, trusted proxies, readiness and graceful shutdown), containers and non-root runtime, Fastify and pino defaults (we use Hono), profiling and `AsyncLocalStorage` practice.
- **Frontend:** TanStack Query and its key and mutation rules, React Hook Form, Tailwind, Next.js, auth tokens, virtualization, live connections, i18n and message catalogs, MSW (the AI is faked at our own boundary).
- **UI/UX:** A/B testing, HEART and SUS metrics, scheduled user-testing rounds, native-platform guidance, tables, search, multi-step forms, password rules, Core Web Vitals targets, right-to-left and translation stress tests, consent and dark-pattern rules, media captions.
- **General:** money and time-zone rules, thread-safety rules.

## Agent roles and models

| Role | Model | Does | Does not |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Orchestrator** | Sonnet | Talks to the user, splits work, writes handoff briefs, integrates results, runs `pnpm check`, owns commits | Large implementations itself; design-heavy planning |
| **Planner / Reviewer** | Opus | Plans non-trivial or cross-cutting work; reviews diffs against these rules and the decision IDs | Write the implementation; run long builds |
| **Builder** | Haiku | Implements one well-bounded task from a brief; writes its tests | Make design decisions, change contracts, touch files outside its brief |

Flow: Orchestrator -> (Opus plan, if needed) -> Haiku build -> Opus review (non-trivial changes, or anything touching `shared/`, `server/` or the editor plugins) -> Orchestrator integrates.

Escalate instead of guessing: a builder that hits an ambiguity, a contract change or a rule conflict stops and reports to the orchestrator.

## Handoffs: cold starts and token efficiency

Side agents start with **no memory of the conversation**. Every handoff carries exactly what they need and nothing more.

**Orchestrator, when handing off:**
- Pass **file paths and decision IDs, not pasted contents.** The agent reads what it needs.
- Name the **minimum reading list** (usually 1-3 files plus the relevant IDs). Never tell a builder to read all of `docs/` or `guidelines/`; the rules a builder needs are in this file.
- State the **scope as a whitelist of files** it may create or edit, and what is out of bounds.
- Give **checkable acceptance criteria** (a test passes, `pnpm check` is green, a specific behavior).
- One task per brief, small enough to finish in one pass. Split large work into independent briefs with no shared files, each step building and passing checks before the next.
- Ask for a **short, structured return** so the result is cheap to read back.

**Brief template:**

```
Task: <one sentence>
Why: <decision IDs, e.g. D4, T5>
Read first: <paths, max ~3>
May edit/create: <file whitelist>
Do not touch: <paths or areas>
Done when: <checkable criteria; include `pnpm check` green>
Return: files changed, one line per change, anything unresolved. No code dumps.
```

**Builder, on start:** read the brief, then only the listed files; do not explore the repo or re-read docs unless told. Follow neighboring patterns. Do not widen scope; note adjacent problems in the return instead of fixing them. Run `pnpm check` before returning and report failures verbatim and briefly.

**Reviewer (Opus), on start:** receive the diff and the decision IDs it should satisfy, not the history. Check against these rules and the cited IDs; report findings ranked by severity with file and line. Do not rewrite code.

**Return format (all side agents):**

```
Status: done | blocked | partial
Changed: <path>: <what, one line>
Checks: <pnpm check result>
Open: <questions, risks, follow-ups>
```

## Context hygiene

- Keep this file and the briefs short; long context costs tokens on every cold start.
- Record durable decisions in `docs/` (with an ID), not in chat. A decision that exists only in a conversation is lost to the next agent.
- When a rule here changes, update this file in the same change.

## Git

Work on `development`; `main` is for releases. Short, imperative commit messages. Add one dependency or one upgrade per commit. The raw AI session files in `ai-sessions/` are added last, unedited except for masked secrets, as the brief requires.

# AGENTS.md

Working rules for AI agents and people in this repo. **Draft: this will evolve as the product grows.** If a rule is wrong or in the way, say so and propose a change instead of working around it.

Priority: user instruction > this file and `docs/` > `guidelines/`. `Never` = hard rule. The full general guidelines are in `guidelines/` (CODING, NODEJS, REACT, UIUX); this file is the project-adapted distillation. **Do not read `guidelines/` by default**; open one only when this file is silent on something.

## Project in one paragraph

A browser-based Markdown editor where an AI co-author flags and suggests; the user always sees a diff and must Accept. React + Vite + TipTap front end, a small Hono proxy to OpenRouter, localStorage persistence, no auth, no database. Pre-implementation: decisions exist, code does not yet.

## Source of truth

Read only what the task needs, not everything.

| Need | File |
|---|---|
| What the product does (D1-D17 editor, H1-H7 home) | `docs/PRODUCT-DIRECTION.md` |
| Stack, AI contract, storage, security, structure, packages, gates (T1-T13) | `docs/TECHNICAL-DIRECTION.md` |
| Tokens, components, licenses, responsive (S1-S9) | `docs/DESIGN-DIRECTION.md` |

Product decisions are settled. Do not re-open them; if code contradicts one, flag it. Cite decision IDs (`D4`, `H5`, `T7`, `S8`) in code comments and test names.

## Project rules

1. **Nothing changes the document without Accept** (T3). Suggestions are decorations; Accept is one transaction.
2. **Contracts live in `shared/schemas/`** as zod, types from `z.infer` (T11). Never hand-duplicate a type.
3. **The OpenRouter key never reaches the browser** (T4). Model names come from config, never from the client (T7).
4. **Model output is untrusted** (T10): validate with zod, render as text only, drop responses whose paragraph hash no longer matches.
5. **Feature code imports UI only from `src/design-system/`**, never `@atlaskit/*` or icon packages directly (S8).
6. **Only permissive licenses** (Apache-2.0, MIT, ISC, BSD). `@atlaskit/icon` and `@atlaskit/logo` are banned; icons are Lucide or custom SVG (S6, S8).
7. **No hover-only affordances**; every interaction has a touch and keyboard path (S9, D17).
8. **No test calls the real model** (T9). Never commit `.env` or secrets. Never log document text or the API key.

## The gate

One command, `pnpm check`, runs: format check, type-aware strict ESLint, `tsc --noEmit`, license check (S8), Vitest, production build (web and server). **It is created before any feature code.**

- Done only when `pnpm check` passes. Fix causes; never suppress errors or warnings (`@ts-ignore`, `eslint-disable`, `any`, non-null `!` need a written reason).
- After every change run the fast checks (format, lint, types). Run tests by scope: affected tests per step, the full suite once before push or done.
- ESLint errors on: undeclared and unused names, shadowing, floating promises, explicit `any`, missing types, `react-hooks` violations, deep imports across features, direct `@atlaskit/*` imports. No `console.log` left behind.
- Report what was run and the real result. Never claim unverified work passes.

## Packages (T12)

- **pnpm only.** Never npm or yarn; never commit another lockfile. Commands: `pnpm dev`, `pnpm test`, `pnpm check`.
- **Exact versions only.** `.npmrc` has `save-exact=true`. No `^`, `~`, ranges or `latest`, dev dependencies included. `packageManager` and `engines` pin pnpm and Node.
- Commit `pnpm-lock.yaml`; install with `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`.
- Adding a dependency: first prefer the platform, the standard library or code we already have. Verify the exact name exists and is maintained, check its license (S8), add one package at a time, run `pnpm check`, commit alone.
- Upgrading: deliberate, one package at a time, license re-checked, checks run, committed alone. `pnpm audit` shows no high or critical findings.
- Dependency install scripts stay blocked unless explicitly allowlisted with a reason.
- Wrap third-party libraries in an adapter when they touch domain logic (AI provider, storage, design system).

## Coding rules

- Read related files before editing; match existing patterns, naming and style. Take the first option that works: not needed -> reuse -> standard library -> platform feature -> installed dependency -> small edit -> new minimal code.
- Smallest diff that fully solves the task. Never refactor, rename or reformat unrelated code. Before changing a signature or schema, find and update every caller.
- Never leave TODOs, stubs, mock data, dead code, commented-out code or debug output. A deliberate shortcut gets one `DEBT:` comment with its limit and when to revisit.
- Never invent APIs, flags or package names; verify in the repo, lockfile or docs. Never deprecated APIs.
- Bug: reproduce it, fix the root cause, not the symptom. Stuck after two attempts at the same fix: stop, report what failed, propose options.
- Ambiguous requirement: pick the simplest option and state the assumption.
- KISS, YAGNI. Abstract on the third repetition; duplication beats a wrong abstraction. One responsibility per function and module. Pure core, side effects at the edges. Composition over inheritance.
- Functions: one level of abstraction, guard clauses over nesting (at most ~3 levels), at most ~4 parameters, no boolean flag parameters, no hidden inputs or outputs.
- Names state intent; units in the name (`timeout_ms`); no magic numbers or strings. No `utils`/`helpers` dumping grounds: name modules by what they own (`diff`, `hash`).
- Types: strictest checking, no escape hatches. Parse external data at the boundary (API, storage, environment) into validated types, then trust them. Discriminated unions instead of flag combinations; `as const` objects instead of `enum`; immutable by default.
- Errors: never swallow (no empty `catch`). Expected failures are typed results; exceptions are for bugs. Messages state what failed, without secrets. Handle edges: empty, missing, zero, duplicate, non-ASCII.
- Never global mutable state or side effects at import time. Inject IO, clock, randomness and environment at the edges; wrap `window`, `localStorage` and the clock in a module or hook.
- Whatever a scope acquires (listener, timer, request, subscription) the same scope releases, on every path.
- Bound everything: input size, retries, timeouts, caches. Measure before optimizing.
- Comments explain why, not what. Document public APIs: purpose, inputs, errors.

## Frontend rules (React)

- Feature-first per T11: components (UI) / hooks (logic) / API client (IO). Never `fetch` in a component. One component per file; split files over ~200 lines. Never define a component inside another.
- Import direction: `app -> features -> design-system / lib`. Other features are reached only through their `index.ts`.
- TypeScript `strict` and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. No `as` casts to silence errors, no `React.FC`. Variants and async state (idle, loading, ready, error) are discriminated unions.
- State at the lowest scope that works: local -> lifted -> URL -> context -> Zustand. Derive values in render; never mirror props or derived data in state. Editor-internal state belongs to the ProseMirror plugins (T3), not React state.
- Effects only synchronize with external systems and always have full deps and cleanup. Never use effects for derived state, event logic or fetching. Reset with `key`. No `useMemo`/`useCallback`/`memo` by default; add after profiling.
- AI calls go through the typed client in `features/ai`: timeout, abort `signal` on every request, one normalized error shape. Handle loading, error, empty and success. AI failure shows the D14 status and never breaks the editor.
- Stable `key` from ids, never the index. Never render `count && <X />`. Dates, numbers and relative times through `Intl`.
- Error boundary per route and around the editor, with fallback and retry. Boundaries do not catch event-handler or async errors; handle those where they occur.
- Security: never `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`; never render user, API or LLM content as HTML or Markdown without sanitizing (T10). No secrets in client code. External `target="_blank"` gets `rel="noopener noreferrer"`. No inline scripts, `eval` or `new Function`.
- Route-level `lazy` + `Suspense`; check bundle cost before adding a library.
- Tests: Vitest + React Testing Library + `user-event`, colocated as `Component.test.tsx`. Query by role, label or text (`data-testid` last). Never test internal state or class names. `findBy*`/`waitFor` and fake timers (for the D4 pause), never fixed sleeps. The AI is faked at the client boundary. Cover loading, error, empty and success.

## Server rules (Hono, Node)

- ESM only. Layers: route (thin) -> AI service -> `AIProvider`. Request and response objects never enter the service. The app is built by a factory with its dependencies passed in (`createApp(deps)`); a separate entrypoint listens.
- Validate body, params and query with zod at the boundary, reject unknown fields, and serialize responses through schemas (T5).
- Environment is parsed once at startup into a typed config; never read `process.env` elsewhere (T7). Fail fast on missing config.
- One error handler maps typed errors to status codes with one body shape; never send stack traces. Out-of-credit maps to the D14 status.
- Every outbound call has a timeout (`AbortSignal.timeout`) and is cancelled when the client disconnects. Retries are bounded (T5: one).
- Never block the event loop: no `*Sync` calls on request paths. Every promise is awaited or handled; `return await` inside `try`.
- Body size limit and model allowlist enforced here (T7). CORS: same-origin through the Vite proxy; allow only the local dev origin.
- Structured logs to stdout with secrets and document text redacted. Never `eval`, `new Function` or `vm`.
- Tests: the service is unit-tested with a fake `AIProvider`; routes through Hono's in-process request against the factory app. Tests close what they open.

## UI/UX rules

- **Done means seen.** Every screen is looked at rendered (screenshot in the browser pane), not only read as code. Check at 360, 768 and 1280px, light and dark, keyboard only, and 200% zoom. Accessibility check clean once automated (axe or similar); until then a manual keyboard and screen-reader pass. Contrast meets WCAG AA.
- Every data view has loading, empty, error and success states (H6, D14).
- Heuristics that matter here: visible system status (feedback in 100 ms, progress after 1 s, e.g. the card spinner); user control (Accept, Dismiss, Esc, single-step undo D17); error prevention (destructive actions confirm and name the object, H5); recovery (say what happened and how to fix, keep the user's input); consistency (reuse design-system components, never restyle one-off); minimal (one primary action per screen).
- Layout: spacing, sizes and radii from tokens only (S2). No horizontal scroll at 320px; fully usable from 360px (S9). Document text at least 16px with 45-75 characters per line; UI chrome follows the ADS scale. Touch targets at least 44x44 on coarse pointers. Reserve space for async content so layout never shifts.
- Color: semantic tokens only, never raw hex; never color alone to carry meaning (S7). Hover, focus, active, selected, disabled and error states are visibly distinct.
- Buttons act, links navigate; button labels are verbs naming the outcome. Modals are rare (delete confirm only): focus trapped, `Esc` closes, focus returns to the trigger. No toast as the only place an error appears.
- **Disabled controls: the product record wins.** H2 and H3 keep visible, disabled items (a promise of future features); give each a small "Soon" label or tooltip so it explains itself.
- Accessibility: semantic HTML first, ARIA only to fill gaps. Everything reachable and operable by keyboard with a visible focus ring; icon-only controls have accessible names; headings and landmarks are hierarchical; async updates use live regions; hover content is also reachable by focus and touch. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- Motion explains cause and effect: 150-300 ms, transform and opacity only, never blocking input.
- Content: plain language, sentence case, one term per concept. The AI speaks in neutral, factual one-liners (D8). Never put a placeholder where a label belongs.

## Dropped on purpose (does not fit this project yet)

Revisit when the product grows (Phase 2: sign-in, sync, real users).

- **Server:** PostgreSQL and the data layer, migrations, idempotency keys, durable job queues, authentication and authorization (JWT, passwords, sessions, cookies), multi-instance concerns (shared rate-limit store, trusted proxies, readiness and graceful shutdown), containers and non-root runtime, Fastify and pino defaults (we use Hono), profiling and `AsyncLocalStorage` practice.
- **Frontend:** TanStack Query and its key and mutation rules, React Hook Form, Tailwind, Next.js, auth tokens, virtualization, live connections, i18n and message catalogs, MSW (the AI is faked at our own boundary).
- **UI/UX:** A/B testing, HEART and SUS metrics, scheduled user-testing rounds, native-platform guidance, tables, search, multi-step forms, password rules, Core Web Vitals targets, right-to-left and translation stress tests, consent and dark-pattern rules, media captions.
- **General:** money and time-zone rules, thread-safety rules.

## Agent roles and models

| Role | Model | Does | Does not |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Orchestrator** | Sonnet | Talks to the user, splits work, writes handoff briefs, integrates results, runs `pnpm check`, owns commits | Large implementations itself; design-heavy planning |
| **Planner / Reviewer** | Opus | Plans non-trivial or cross-cutting work; reviews diffs against these rules and the decision IDs | Write the implementation; run long builds |
| **Builder** | Haiku | Implements one well-bounded task from a brief; writes its tests | Make design decisions, change contracts, touch files outside its brief |

Flow: Orchestrator -> (Opus plan, if needed) -> Haiku build -> Opus review (non-trivial changes, or anything touching `shared/`, `server/` or the editor plugins) -> Orchestrator integrates.

Escalate instead of guessing: a builder that hits an ambiguity, a contract change or a rule conflict stops and reports to the orchestrator.

## Handoffs: cold starts and token efficiency

Side agents start with **no memory of the conversation**. Every handoff carries exactly what they need and nothing more.

**Orchestrator, when handing off:**
- Pass **file paths and decision IDs, not pasted contents.** The agent reads what it needs.
- Name the **minimum reading list** (usually 1-3 files plus the relevant IDs). Never tell a builder to read all of `docs/` or `guidelines/`; the rules a builder needs are in this file.
- State the **scope as a whitelist of files** it may create or edit, and what is out of bounds.
- Give **checkable acceptance criteria** (a test passes, `pnpm check` is green, a specific behavior).
- One task per brief, small enough to finish in one pass. Split large work into independent briefs with no shared files, each step building and passing checks before the next.
- Ask for a **short, structured return** so the result is cheap to read back.

**Brief template:**

```
Task: <one sentence>
Why: <decision IDs, e.g. D4, T5>
Read first: <paths, max ~3>
May edit/create: <file whitelist>
Do not touch: <paths or areas>
Done when: <checkable criteria; include `pnpm check` green>
Return: files changed, one line per change, anything unresolved. No code dumps.
```

**Builder, on start:** read the brief, then only the listed files; do not explore the repo or re-read docs unless told. Follow neighboring patterns. Do not widen scope; note adjacent problems in the return instead of fixing them. Run `pnpm check` before returning and report failures verbatim and briefly.

**Reviewer (Opus), on start:** receive the diff and the decision IDs it should satisfy, not the history. Check against these rules and the cited IDs; report findings ranked by severity with file and line. Do not rewrite code.

**Return format (all side agents):**

```
Status: done | blocked | partial
Changed: <path>: <what, one line>
Checks: <pnpm check result>
Open: <questions, risks, follow-ups>
```

## Context hygiene

- Keep this file and the briefs short; long context costs tokens on every cold start.
- Record durable decisions in `docs/` (with an ID), not in chat. A decision that exists only in a conversation is lost to the next agent.
- When a rule here changes, update this file in the same change.

## Git

Work on `development`; `main` is for releases. Short, imperative commit messages. Add one dependency or one upgrade per commit. The raw AI session files in `ai-sessions/` are added last, unedited except for masked secrets, as the brief requires.

- Give **checkable acceptance criteria** (a test passes, `pnpm check` is green, a specific behavior).

Why: <decision IDs, e.g. D4, T5>
Read first: <paths, max ~3>

**Return format (all side agents):**

```
Status: done | blocked | partial
Changed: <path>: <what, one line>
Checks: <pnpm check result>
Open: <questions, risks, follow-ups>
```

- Keep this file and the briefs short; long context costs tokens on every cold start.
- Record durable decisions in `docs/` (with an ID), not in chat. A decision that exists only in a conversation is lost to the next agent.
- When a rule here changes, update this file in the same change.

## Git

Work on `development`; `main` is for releases. Short, imperative commit messages. Add one dependency or one upgrade per commit. The raw AI session files in `ai-sessions/` are added last, unedited except for masked secrets, as the brief requires.

# AI Co-Author Editor

A collaborative AI document editor in the browser. You write Markdown; an AI co-author notices things, speaks up quietly, and never changes the document without a visible diff and your explicit Accept.

> **Status: pre-implementation.** Product, technical and design decisions are written down; no application code exists yet. This README is a working draft and will evolve with the product.

## What it is

- A home screen listing your documents (create, open, delete), then a Markdown editor.
- **Ambient mode:** the AI flags passages with subtle underlines (clarity, tone, grammar, questions to the author). **On demand mode:** you invoke it on a selection, a section, or with `/`.
- Suggestions appear as an anchored card with a live inline diff. You Accept, Dismiss or Refine (tone, length, free instruction). Nothing is written until Accept.
- Section restructuring (move, split, merge) with the same preview-then-accept flow.
- Documents and version history are saved in the browser. No account, no database.

Full detail: [docs/PRODUCT-DIRECTION.md](docs/PRODUCT-DIRECTION.md).

## Stack

TypeScript, React, Vite, TipTap (ProseMirror), a small Hono server that proxies AI calls to OpenRouter, Vitest. Details and reasons: [docs/TECHNICAL-DIRECTION.md](docs/TECHNICAL-DIRECTION.md). Design system: [docs/DESIGN-DIRECTION.md](docs/DESIGN-DIRECTION.md).

## Run it locally

*Planned; these commands work once the project is scaffolded.*

Requirements: Node 20+, an OpenRouter API key.

```bash
pnpm install
cp .env.example .env   # then set OPENROUTER_API_KEY
pnpm dev            # starts the web app and the AI proxy
```

Other commands:

```bash
pnpm test               # unit tests (Vitest)
pnpm check          # typecheck + lint + license check + tests
```

The API key stays on the local server and is never sent to the browser.

## Repository map

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `docs/` | Product, technical and design direction |
| `mockups/` | Medium-fidelity prototype (visual reference only) |
| `AGENTS.md` | Working rules for AI agents and contributors |
| `ai-sessions/` | Raw AI session files, added at the end as the brief requires |

The planned source layout is in [docs/TECHNICAL-DIRECTION.md](docs/TECHNICAL-DIRECTION.md).

## What I'd do differently with more time

To be written when the build is done.

content.text:
I've read all four guidelines and folded them into [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md), which is now 176 lines. Nothing is committed yet.

**How they're used**
- **Distilled, not copied:** `guidelines/` stays as your full reference. AGENTS.md says not to read it by default, so cold-start agents load one short file instead of about 400 lines.
- **Gate:** `pnpm check` is the single done-condition. It runs format, strict type-aware ESLint, `tsc`, the license check, Vitest and the production build, and it is created before any feature code.
- **Rules:** the coding, React, server (Hono) and UI/UX rules are rewritten for this project. Examples are the AI client with timeouts and abort, text-only rendering of AI output, and "done means seen" at 360, 768 and 1280px.

**Dropped on purpose (listed in AGENTS.md for later)**
- **Server:** the database and migrations, auth, queues, multi-instance and container rules, and the Fastify and pino defaults.
- **Frontend:** TanStack Query, React Hook Form, Tailwind, Next.js and i18n.
- **UI/UX:** A/B tests and HEART/SUS metrics, native-platform guidance, tables, multi-step forms and consent rules.

**Where the guidelines conflicted with product decisions**
- **Disabled controls:** the guidelines say to avoid them, but H2 and H3 keep them visible as a promise of future features. The product wins, and each gets a small "Soon" label or tooltip so it explains itself.
- **Body text size:** the guidelines want at least 16px. I applied that to document text, and UI chrome follows the ADS scale.

**Packages and docs**
- **pnpm only, exact versions (T12):** `.npmrc` sets `save-exact=true` with no `^` or `~`, and `packageManager` and `engines` pin pnpm and Node. The lockfile is committed and installs use `--frozen-lockfile`. Each dependency or upgrade is one package at a time and committed alone, with the licence re-checked.
- **Docs updated:** T12 and T13 are added to the technical doc, and the README and docs now use pnpm. The README gains env vars and known limits, per the coding guidelines' delivery rules.
- **Lima:** I kept it out of the docs and saved it as a private note, so the missing Node and pnpm on the host are not treated as a blocker.

# AI Co-Author Editor

A collaborative AI document editor in the browser. You write Markdown; an AI co-author notices things, speaks up quietly, and never changes the document without a visible diff and your explicit Accept.

> **Status: pre-implementation.** Product, technical and design decisions are written down; no application code exists yet. This README is a working draft and will evolve with the product.

## What it is

- A home screen listing your documents (create, open, delete), then a Markdown editor.
- **Ambient mode:** the AI flags passages with subtle underlines (clarity, tone, grammar, questions to the author). **On demand mode:** you invoke it on a selection, a section, or with `/`.
- Suggestions appear as an anchored card with a live inline diff. You Accept, Dismiss or Refine (tone, length, free instruction). Nothing is written until Accept.
- Section restructuring (move, split, merge) with the same preview-then-accept flow.
- Documents and version history are saved in the browser. No account, no database.

Full detail: [docs/PRODUCT-DIRECTION.md](docs/PRODUCT-DIRECTION.md).

## Stack

TypeScript, React, Vite, TipTap (ProseMirror), a small Hono server that proxies AI calls to OpenRouter, Vitest. Details and reasons: [docs/TECHNICAL-DIRECTION.md](docs/TECHNICAL-DIRECTION.md). Design system: [docs/DESIGN-DIRECTION.md](docs/DESIGN-DIRECTION.md).

## Run it locally

*Planned; these commands work once the project is scaffolded.*

Requirements: Node (version pinned in `.nvmrc`), pnpm (version pinned in `packageManager`; enable it with `corepack enable`), an OpenRouter API key.

```bash
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
cp .env.example .env   # then set OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model names
pnpm dev               # starts the web app and the AI proxy
```

Other commands:

```bash
pnpm test              # unit tests (Vitest)
pnpm check             # format + lint + types + license check + tests + build
```

Dependencies are pinned to exact versions and installed from the committed lockfile.

The API key stays on the local server and is never sent to the browser.

## Environment variables

Listed in `.env.example` once scaffolded: `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, one model name per AI task (analyze, rewrite, restructure), and the input size cap.

## Repository map

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `docs/` | Product, technical and design direction |
| `mockups/` | Medium-fidelity prototype (visual reference only) |
| `AGENTS.md` | Working rules for AI agents and contributors (adapted from `guidelines/`) |
| `guidelines/` | Full general coding, Node, React and UI/UX guidelines (reference) |
| `ai-sessions/` | Raw AI session files, added at the end as the brief requires |

The planned source layout is in [docs/TECHNICAL-DIRECTION.md](docs/TECHNICAL-DIRECTION.md).

## Known limits

- Single user, single browser: documents live in localStorage, so there is no sync or sharing.
- The AI proxy is public-facing only if you deploy it; it is built for local use, with a size cap and model allowlist but no per-IP rate limit.
- Markdown round-trips through the editor can normalize formatting.

## What I'd do differently with more time

To be written when the build is done.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- anthropic-skills:built-in-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:chrome-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:computer-use: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills.
- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:deep-research: Use this skill when the user's prompt requires (1) researching a topic across multiple sources, comparing options or alternatives, analyzing trends or history, understanding markets or industries, or reviewing literature or studies and (2) synthesizing that research into a comprehensive, narrative report. If you're planning to search the web or internal knowledge bases, consider using this skill. This skill coordinates research subagents, so use it only when you have a tool for spawning subagents (the Agent or Task tool); otherwise, research the question directly.
- anthropic-skills:docs: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:explain-usage: Explain where this session's tokens went, with one simple chart in plain language. Use when the user says things like "explain my usage", "where did my tokens go", or asks for a usage breakdown.
- anthropic-skills:google-workspace: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files.
- anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:setup-claude: Guided setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
